steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Specialisation means focusing on producing a limited range of goods or services — individuals, firms, and countries can all specialise.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Division of labour breaks production into separate tasks, with each worker performing one task. Adam Smith identified this as a key source of productivity gains.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Benefits: increased productivity, time saved (no switching tasks), specialist equipment, higher output and lower unit costs.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Costs: worker boredom and demotivation, over-dependence on one product or market, skills become obsolete if the industry changes.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain three benefits and two costs of the division of labour for workers and firms. | Analyse why specialisation leads to exchange and interdependence. | Evaluate whether the benefits of specialisation always outweigh the costs.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always give BOTH benefits AND costs of specialisation. Link specialisation to TRADE: specialisation creates the need for exchange. Adam Smith's pin factory is the classic example of division of labour.
